text.p: Germany's economic recovery is gaining ground, with growth of one percent expected this year and 2.5 percent next year, the Institute of the German Economy (IW) said on Wednesday.

The forecast put the Cologne-based IW roughly in line with a broadening consensus on the outlook for Europe's largest economy. The latest Reuter survey of over 30 economists showed they on average expected growth of 1.2 percent this year and 2.2 percent in 1997.

In its forecast for 1997, the IW institute said expansion would be led by exports and capital investment. But consumer demand will only grow moderately and unemployment will stay at a stubbornly high average of four million.
The IW sees inflationary pressures remaining subdued, with consumer price growth seen at 1.5 percent in 1996 and 1997.
"A precondition (for recovery) is that economic and wage policy is aimed at reducing the competitive disadvantages of the German economy against its competitors," it said.
Continued weakness in the building sector -- important in former-communist eastern Germany -- will act as a brake on the recovery, it added.

The latest Ifo institute survey of business confidence, released on Wednesday, also showed an improvement in confidence to the highest level in about a year, although the outlook for east German manufacturers remained gloomy.
And the BDI Federation of German Industry also said in its latest economic outlook that activity picked up around the middle of the year, with both orders and output on the up.
But the BDI said it was too early to declare the "patient economy" healed because the recovery in the second quarter of this year was exaggerated due to a weather-hit winter.
"The economy continues to lack a leg on which to base a recovery besides exports," the BDI said in a statement.
